extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of 19th-century humorous essays and poetry (literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Oliver Wendell Holmes' Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table containing observations on voice, poetry, and poetic habits; useful as informal craft guidance for writers of humorous essays and lyric poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of floral imagery and repetition in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets naturally and repeatedly use flowers and floral imagery; omission of such images would seem odd. "Do you ever wonder why poets talk so much about flowers? Did you ever hear of a poet who did not talk about them?... No,—they will bloom over and over again in poems as in the summer fields, to the end of time, always old and always new."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat floral imagery as conventional but legitimate material — repetition is not weakness but part of the poet’s repertory (compared to Nature endlessly repeating blossoms). The text argues against an anti-repetition aesthetic: poets need not avoid familiar images for fear of being unoriginal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept leaving traces/roots of composition in verse
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet’s remark that one should not read certain verses too literally and that he likes to "keep [the roots], and a little of the soil clinging to them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow some rawness, origin-markers, or 'roots' to remain in a poem rather than over-polishing everything. Antipattern: trimming so carefully that all sense of origin or lived material is lost. Readers/critics should avoid overly literal readings that strip away the poet’s intended texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a single memorable line to many ephemeral epigrams
rubrics_metrics.description: The Professor’s principle: he would "rather write a single line which one among them should think worth remembering than set them all laughing with a string of epigrams."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for durability and depth in poetic expression rather than seeking immediate laughter or a parade of clever but forgettable quips. Scoring note: lasting resonance (a memorable line) is valued over transient comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve authentic, idiosyncratic voice in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator refuses to 'change his peculiar expressions' of a young fellow because 'this is one of those cases in which the style is the man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering speech or character, retain original colloquialisms and eccentricities: they convey character and authenticity. Anti-pattern: sanitizing or standardizing dialect and peculiarities, which erases personality and flattens characterization.
